title: Crypto controls & audit log workshop - Echo Pharmaceutics
summary: Workshop to align Echo Pharmaceutics' crypto controls with Redwood Private and Dedicated options. Covered BYOK/HSM integration paths, key rotation and escrow approaches, audit log structure and retention policies, RBAC/SSO mapping for operations, and regional data residency implications. Agreed to run a short benchmark and produce a design doc for HSM connector options and an SOC2 evidence checklist.

Arun Patel (Echo) - Provide current key rotation policy and sample KMS IAM roles by 2026-05-24
Nina Flores (Echo) - Confirm required audit log retention period (legal/compliance) by 2026-05-22
Jordan Myers (Redwood) - Share security whitepaper and SOC2 artifact map by 2026-05-21

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-19
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Myers (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samira Khan (Echo Head of Security), Dr. Luis Mendez (Echo CTO), Arun Patel (Cloud Architect), Nina Flores (Compliance Manager)

Summary (auto): High-level review of encryption, BYOK/HSM options, audit log and retention needs, RBAC/SSO mapping, and next steps to run a pilot.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Myers: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. this is Jordan from Redwood. we've got Priya with me on the technical side. how are you all?
[00:07] Samira Khan: Hi Jordan, hi Priya. good, thanks. we've got a couple people on our side, I'll let Luis intro himself.
[00:12] Dr. Luis Mendez: Yeah hi everyone, I'm Luis, CTO here at Echo Pharmaceutics. we run most of our workloads in a multi-region cloud account, us-east and eu-west, and we're looking at Redwood for inference across PHI-adjacent workloads.
[00:25] Arun Patel: Arun here, cloud architect. today we want to understand how keys are managed, who has access, and what the audit trail looks like for regulatory review.
[00:34] Priya Nair: Great, that's exactly what we planned to cover. We'll walk through encryption at rest and in transit, BYOK and HSM options for Private deploys, audit logs, and RBAC/SSO integration. Also any residency or segmentation questions.
[00:44] Nina Flores: Quick note, compliance side: our legal team requires 7 years retention for certain audit records, and we need ability to show key custody proofs during audits.
[00:52] Jordan Myers: Noted, 7 years is pretty long. we'll talk retention architecture that supports long-term logs.
[00:58] [01:02] Priya Nair: To start, a quick overview: Redwood Private supports two patterns for customer keys. One is cloud-KMS BYOK where you upload or grant access to keys in your cloud KMS and we call the service with envelope encryption. The other is HSM peering or connector - an HSM-backed key store where master wrap keys never leave your HSM.
[01:22] Priya Nair: Important nuance — in the HSM connector pattern, Redwood's runtime uses short-lived wrapping keys provided via the connector for each pod/instance; the master key stays in customer H S M. there is also an escrow and rotation path we can configure.
[01:36] Arun Patel: A couple quick questions: we use a dedicated VPC, can the HSM connector go over a private peering link? and can we bring our own HSM (we're evaluating Thales and AWS CloudHSM)?
[01:48] Priya Nair: Yes, private peering is supported for Redwood Private. For BYOK, we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and Azure Key Vault with role-based grants. For HSM we support HSM peering with FIPS 140-2 Level 3 compliant HSMs; we've done connectors for both vendor-HSMs and cloud-HSMs.
[02:04] Samira Khan: There's often confusion on rotation responsibilities. who rotates the key and how do we prove to auditors that rotation happened?
[02:12] Jordan Myers: Good Q. We recommend customer-managed rotation for master keys so you control rotation cadence and have the audit trail. Redwood can rotate intermediate wrapping keys automatically and emits an audit event for each rotation. We'll map those events to the audit log entries.
[02:26] [02:40] Dr. Luis Mendez: Can you give an example of the audit entries? what's included?
[02:44] Priya Nair: Sure. Each crypto event includes time, operation (encrypt/decrypt/rotate), key ID (customer key reference), the wrapping key fingerprint, the Redwood node id, request ID, and associated token or tenant id. We also log the request's TLS term and cipher suite, though low-level cipher details can be redacted per policy.
[03:10] Arun Patel: How are logs shipped? we have retention needs and want immutability, ideally WORM style or sent to our SIEM.
[03:18] Priya Nair: Redwood supports multiple sinks: push to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver/EventHub, direct S3/GCS transfer to a locked bucket with bucket policies, and syslog/remote SIEM ingest. For immutability we can recommend S3 Object Lock or a Write-Once retention on your side. Redwood's audit logs are also signed and can include a chain-of-trust header to help with tamper evidence.
[03:38] Samira Khan: That's helpful. Could you clarify what evidence Redwood provides for SOC2? we need controls mapping.
[03:46] Jordan Myers: We'll send the SOC2 artifact map. Practically speaking: we provide signed audit logs, access logs for the control plane, RBAC change events, and config snapshots for infra changes.
[03:56] [04:12] Nina Flores: On data residency: we must ensure that key material for EU customers stays in eu-west. do you support geo-fenced HSMs?
[04:21] Priya Nair: Yes. In Private we can configure regional HSM connectors. The master key can be created and stored in the target region's HSM and never replicated out. Redwood runtime will route requests to the regional pool according to policy. There's an obvious latency tradeoff if the serving pool is in a different region.
[04:40] Arun Patel: Which approach gives better latency/costs — cloud-KMS BYOK vs HSM peering?
[04:47] Priya Nair: Cloud KMS is simpler and often lower operational cost but it introduces an additional network hop to KMS for key unwrap in some patterns. HSM peering keeps master keys local but requires dedicated networking and potentially higher ops overhead. For high-throughput inference we typically recommend envelope encryption with a lightweight local wrapping cache to avoid per-request KMS round-trips. That reduces token cost and latency.
[05:16] [05:30] Jordan Myers: Quick interjection — we've seen customers use a hybrid: master key in cloud-KMS but nightly rotation/backup key copies in HSM escrow for disaster recovery. that pattern satisfies certain auditors who want an offline copy.
[05:40] Samira Khan: On BYOK, what are the permissions we need to grant? we don't want to give broad decrypt rights if possible.
[05:47] Priya Nair: For envelope encryption, Redwood needs the ability to generate data keys (kms:GenerateDataKey) and optionally decrypt if we need to unwrap in the service. We can also do a pattern where Redwood only holds encrypted blobs and unwrap happens in a small, customer-controlled proxy — but that adds latency and a small integration. We can scope permissions to a single key and restrict to our service principal.
[06:06] [06:30] Arun Patel: About key rotation and forensic requirements: we sometimes need to provide per-request proofs; can Redwood include the full request trace in the audit log?
[06:39] Priya Nair: We can include a request trace id and event chain. Because of PII/PHI concerns we'll redact payloads, but we can include hashes or fingerprints that allow you to correlate request evidence without storing sensitive content.
[06:53] Dr. Luis Mendez: Any limitations on sequence length or token caching that affect KV cache safety? We're concerned about decrypted KV cache existing in memory on nodes.
[07:02] Priya Nair: Runtime keeps KV cache encrypted at rest and in memory uses memory-protected pages; for additional guarantee we offer ephemeral compute modes and can avoid caching decrypted material in memory between calls. There are tradeoffs with latency. We surface cache options and you can tune tradeoff.
[07:22] [07:40] Jordan Myers: Let's talk operational access: who at Redwood can view keys or decrypted data?
[07:45] Priya Nair: Redwood staff do not have access to customer master keys in BYOK or HSM-peered modes. For hosted defaults we manage keys within our KMS and ops staff have limited emergency access under strict, logged procedures. For Private/HSM the customer retains exclusive control of the master key.
[08:02] Samira Khan: Are there controls for privileged access in the control plane? SSO/SAML, RBAC mapping to our AD?
[08:11] Jordan Myers: Yes we support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning. RBAC is role based and can be mapped to AD groups. We can synchronize groups and map to Redwood roles like infra-admin, security-auditor, etc. All role changes are logged.
[08:26] [08:50] Nina Flores: For audits, we also need to show proof that rotations happened and who initiated them. are rotation events signed?
[08:57] Priya Nair: rotation events are logged and signed. We can produce a time-stamped rotation report showing key versions, crypto fingerprints, and the initiator (user or system).
[09:10] Arun Patel: One of our constraints is offline key escrow for legal hold. how have you handled escrow with other customers?
[09:18] Priya Nair: We've implemented two approaches: (1) customer-managed escrow where keys are exported under strict procedures to an offline HSM module, and (2) third-party escrow where a neutral custodian holds a wrapped copy. Both patterns require formal key-handling runbooks. We'll include recommended runbook text.
[09:38] [09:58] Jordan Myers: Quick commercial note — doing HSM peering for a region adds some setup time (network, certs, runbooks) and usually a one-time onboarding fee. We'll include a rough estimate in the follow-up.
[10:08] Samira Khan: Are there encryption-in-transit specifics? do you support mTLS between Redwood runtime and customer endpoints?
[10:16] Priya Nair: Yes, all inter-service traffic is TLS 1.3 by default. For Private deployments we support mutual TLS with client certs and we can integrate with your internal PKI. We also support TLS certificate pinning for additional assurance.
[10:32] [10:50] Dr. Luis Mendez: For our pilot, what would you need from us to get a realistic benchmark?
[10:56] Priya Nair: We'll need a representative prompt mix, dataset sizes, expected concurrency, and whether PHI is in payloads (redacted ok). Also your target region and whether you want HSM-peering or cloud-KMS pattern tested.
[11:12] Arun Patel: we'll provide a subset of workloads and a short-lived test account with limited permissions.
[11:17] Jordan Myers: Great. we'll run a small bench to measure per-token latency with and without KMS round-trip and show cost delta.
[11:27] [11:50] Samira Khan: Another auditors ask — how do you prove non-repudiation if someone says Redwood changed a key or config?
[11:58] Priya Nair: For critical config changes we keep signed config snapshots with change-set audits. RBAC and change approvals can be enforced via SSO group approvals or a separate change management workflow. We can produce a tamper-evident archive of these snapshots.
[12:16] Nina Flores: Any known vendor limitations? for example, storage formats that make long-term archiving hard?
[12:23] Priya Nair: Logs are exportable in common formats (JSON, NDJSON) and we can hand them off to an archival store. The only limitation sometimes is when logs contain structured embeddings — we typically store hashes to avoid large footprint.
[12:40] [13:00] Arun Patel: What about cross-region failover for keys if primary region is down?
[13:06] Priya Nair: Cross-region failover depends on your key replication policy. If using cloud-KMS and replication is enabled, you can replicate keys to a DR region. For HSM that can't be done without explicit escrow copies. We often recommend a hybrid with an escrowed wrapped key available in DR HSM under strict access controls.
[13:26] Jordan Myers: Ok, let's surface the rough deliverables: Priya will produce HSM connector design, Jordan will send SOC2 artifact map, and we'll propose two integration patterns with estimates. Echo will supply rotation policy and retention requirements.
[13:42] [13:58] Samira Khan: On evidentiary items: can Redwood produce a sample signed audit file and the verification steps so our auditors can validate signatures?
[14:05] Priya Nair: Yes, we'll include a sample signed audit bundle and verification script. We can also run through verification in a follow-up call if auditors want a walkthrough.
[14:16] Arun Patel: one last technical detail — can logs be pushed to our SIEM over TLS with mutual auth and guaranteed delivery?
[14:24] Priya Nair: We support syslog over TLS with client certs and retry semantics. For guaranteed delivery we recommend the S3 sink with Object Lock as a more durable pattern.
[14:42] [15:00] Jordan Myers: Thanks everyone, we're at about 50 minutes. any final Qs?
[15:05] Samira Khan: Nothing further. next steps sound good — interested to see the sample signed bundle.
[15:11] Dr. Luis Mendez: We'll coordinate internally for the pilot data set and send Arun's rotation policy.
[15:16] Nina Flores: I'll confirm the legal retention window and whether 7 years is strict for audit artifacts.
[15:21] Jordan Myers: Perfect. we'll follow up with the docs and schedule the technical deep dive.
[15:27] Priya Nair: Thanks all.
[15:30] Meeting ends.

Notes on transcription quality: Some technical terms transcribed oddly (H S M sometimes split, KV cache transcribed as KV cash), speaker overlap minimal.
